sections.text:
1 Cf. Introductorium Apomasaris, V, 18 (e, 2, edit. 1506) : De puteis stellarum. —
Sunt varii per diversa signa gradus inter adminicula stellarum et obstacula
versantes quorum qui obstant arabica lingua putei stellarum vocantur, quos nos
precipitia dicere solemus.
2 Paulo ab his differunt quae Stephanus philosophus de populis qui astrologiam
coluerunt docet, Catal., II. p. 182.
3 Cf. supra p. 146, n. 1.
4 Ἡ βίβλος Ἰωάννου τοῦ υἱοῦ Μουσούρ περὶ ἀναποδισμῶν καὶ ταπεινώσεων
laudatur in catalogo librorum prohibitorum qui in bibliotheca Chalipharum ser-
vabantur. Catal., I, p. 84, 6. Notus est Jaḥjâ (= Iohannes) ben Abî Manṣûr astro-
logus Persa Chalifae el Manṣûr. Cf. Suter, op. cit., p. 8, n° 14.
5 Muhamed ben el Djâm, aequalis Apomasaris, qui saepe eo auctore utitur, cf.
Suter, Mathematiker der Araber, p. 18, n° 36.
6 Fortasse Ibrahim ben Habîb el Fazâri, primus musulmanorum qui de astro-
logia scripserit, et qui simul cum Omare el Tabarî Bagdadam construxisse fertur;
cf. Suter, op. cit., p. 3, n° 1 et p. 7.
sections.en: 1 Cf. Introductorium Apomasaris, V, 18 (e, 2, edit. 1506) : On the pits of the stars. — There are various degrees through different signs turning between the supports of the stars and the obstacles, of which those that obstruct are called in the Arabic language the pits of the stars, which we are accustomed to call precipices. 2 What Stephen the philosopher teaches concerning the peoples who cultivated astrology differs a little from these, Catal., II. p. 182. 3 Cf. supra p. 146, n. 1. 4 Ἡ βίβλος Ἰωάννου τοῦ υἱοῦ Μουσούρ περὶ ἀναποδισμῶν καὶ ταπεινώσεων ('The book of John the son of Mousour concerning retrogradations and depressions') is praised in the catalogue of prohibited books which were preserved in the library of the Caliphs. Catal., I, p. 84, 6. Jaḥjâ (= Iohannes) ben Abî Manṣûr, a Persian astrologer of the Caliph el Manṣûr, is known. Cf. Suter, op. cit., p. 8, n° 14. 5 Muhamed ben el Djâm, a contemporary of Apomasar, who often uses him as an author, cf. Suter, Mathematiker der Araber, p. 18, n° 36. 6 Perhaps Ibrahim ben Habîb el Fazâri, the first of the Muslims who wrote about astrology, and who is reported to have built Baghdad together with Omar el Tabarî; cf. Suter, op. cit., p. 3, n° 1 and p. 7.

summary.headline: Apomasar on Wells and Aphetas
summary.text: Astrological excerpts from Codex Bruxellensis: Albumasar describes petitionary configurations involving the Dragon’s Head, Jupiter, the Moon, and the ascendant; Apomasar discusses the wells of the stars, the successive peoples who discovered astronomy, and aphetas, citing John son of Mousour, Mouchoumet son of Zachm, and Phizyres.
